topic.subject: social
topic.title: The revolt of 1857
topic.scope: causes, cartridges, Mangal Pandey, Meerut, Bahadur Shah Zafar, leaders at Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, aftermath and Crown rule

misconceptions.statement: The revolt happened only because of the greased cartridges.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the most dramatic immediate cause mentioned in textbooks.
misconceptions.fix: The cartridges were the immediate spark, but deep-seated political, economic, and social grievances had been building for decades.

probe.question: If the British had replaced the cartridges immediately, would the revolt have been completely avoided?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the religious insult was the only reason the sepoys were angry.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: History education research on causal reasoning

misconceptions.statement: The Doctrine of Lapse allowed the British to take over any kingdom whenever they wanted.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the power of the British without understanding the specific legal pretext used.
misconceptions.fix: The Doctrine of Lapse specifically targeted states where the ruler died without a natural male heir, refusing to recognize adopted sons.

probe.question: Could the British use the Doctrine of Lapse to take over a kingdom where the King had a biological son?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they could use it on any kingdom they liked.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule applies to everyone without conditions

misconceptions.statement: Mangal Pandey was the leader who led the sepoys from Meerut to Delhi.
misconceptions.why: He is the most famous individual associated with the start of the unrest, leading to a chronology slip.
misconceptions.fix: Mangal Pandey's action took place in Barrackpore in March; the march from Meerut to Delhi happened in May, led by different sepoys.

probe.question: Where was Mangal Pandey when the sepoys reached the Red Fort in Delhi?
probe.wrong_answer: He was leading them at the gates of the Red Fort.

misconceptions.root_belief: the first person mentioned started the main event

misconceptions.statement: Bahadur Shah Zafar was a powerful military general who planned the revolt.
misconceptions.why: Students assume the 'leader' of a revolt must be its active military commander.
misconceptions.fix: Bahadur Shah Zafar was an elderly, symbolic leader whom the sepoys forced to support them to gain legitimacy.

probe.question: Why did the sepo_ys go to Bahadur Shah Zafar?
probe.wrong_answer: Because he was a great warrior who had a large army ready to fight.

misconceptions.root_belief: the person at the top does everything

misconceptions.statement: Rani Lakshmibai fought because she wanted to create a democratic India.
misconceptions.why: Students project modern political values (democracy/nationalism) onto 19th-century figures.
misconceptions.fix: She fought primarily to protect her kingdom of Jhansi and the rights of her adopted son after the British annexed her state.

probe.question: What was the main goal of Rani Lakshmibai when she joined the rebels?
probe.wrong_answer: To hold elections and make India a democracy.

misconceptions.root_belief: people in the past thought like people today
misconceptions.source_hint: Historical thinking research by Sam Wineburg

misconceptions.statement: The British East India Company continued to rule India until 1947.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse 'The British' as a single entity and don't realize the internal shift from Company to Crown.
misconceptions.fix: After the 1857 revolt, the British Parliament passed an Act in 1858 transferring power from the Company to the British Crown.

probe.question: Who was the official ruler of India in 1860?
probe.wrong_answer: The Governor of the East India Company.

misconceptions.root_belief: major changes only happen at famous dates

misconceptions.statement: Christian missionaries were employees of the British government.
misconceptions.why: Since both were British/European, students assume they were part of the same official organization.
misconceptions.fix: Missionaries were private religious groups, though the British government passed laws that helped them, like allowing them to own land.

probe.question: Did the British government force all sepoys to become Christians?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the missionaries were government officers in charge of the army.

misconceptions.root_belief: all foreigners belong to the same organization

misconceptions.statement: The British increased the number of Indian soldiers in the army to prevent future revolts.
misconceptions.why: Students might think 'more soldiers' equals 'more security' without considering the source of the threat.
misconceptions.fix: The British actually increased the ratio of European soldiers to Indian soldiers to ensure they could control any future mutiny.

probe.question: How did the British change the army after 1857?
probe.wrong_answer: They hired more Indian soldiers because they needed more help to guard the borders.

misconceptions.root_belief: loyalty is rewarded with more responsibility

misconceptions.statement: Nana Saheb was the biological son of the Peshwa.
misconceptions.why: Students often miss the 'adopted' status which was the very reason for his conflict with the British.
misconceptions.fix: Nana Saheb was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II; the British refused him his father's pension because he wasn't a biological heir.

probe.question: Why did the British refuse to pay a pension to Nana Saheb?
probe.wrong_answer: Because he was a bad ruler and they didn't like him.

misconceptions.root_belief: a leader always rules the place they live in

misconceptions.statement: The British continued to annex Indian states using the Doctrine of Lapse after the revolt.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that because the British won, they continued their previous aggressive expansion policies.
misconceptions.fix: To win the loyalty of local rulers, the British promised in 1858 that no more Indian states would be annexed.

probe.question: What happened to the policy of annexation after 1858?
probe.wrong_answer: The British used it even more to punish the rulers who revolted.

misconceptions.root_belief: a policy once started never stops

misconceptions.statement: Only the sepoys were unhappy with the British; the peasants were neutral.
misconceptions.why: The event is often called the 'Sepoy Mutiny', leading students to ignore the civilian participation.
misconceptions.fix: Peasants were deeply unhappy due to high land taxes and loss of land to moneylenders, and they joined the sepoys in the rebellion.

probe.question: Who joined the sepoys in the villages of Awadh?
probe.wrong_answer: No one, the peasants were too busy farming to care about the revolt.

misconceptions.root_belief: a name describes the whole event

misconceptions.statement: The British defeated the rebels easily within a few days.
misconceptions.why: Students often underestimate the scale and duration of historical conflicts once they know the final outcome.
misconceptions.fix: It took the British over a year of heavy fighting and reinforcements from England to fully suppress the revolt.

probe.question: How long did it take for the British to recapture all the major centers of the revolt?
probe.wrong_answer: Just a week after they took back Delhi.
